bracket: [Textbook answer-key error, and the value is wrong by a factor of 100: the printed key gives the volume as \(8.552\) m\(^{3}\). A metal sheet 4.2 m by 1.0 m and 2 cm thick cannot have a volume of 8.5 cubic metres. The key is ALSO quoted to four significant figures in a question that asks for the answer "to correct significant figures", where the 3-figure thickness allows only three; the printed area \(4.255\) m\(^{2}\) is correct on both counts.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the relative error as \(\pm 0.0292\) m s\(^{-1}\). A relative error is a ratio of two quantities carrying the same unit, so it is a pure number and cannot have units — the value \(0.0292\) is correct, the unit is not. The same slip is made again at Q.3 (viii), which makes it systematic rather than a typo.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the relative error as \(0.0065\ \Omega\). A relative error is a ratio of two resistances, so it is dimensionless — the value is correct, the unit is not. The same slip is made at Q.3 (ii). Note the mean absolute error \(0.04\ \Omega\) on the same line is correctly given a unit, since that quantity does have one.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the total mass as \(43\) kg. Both measurements are stated to one decimal place, so the sum must be reported as \(43.0\) kg — dropping the trailing zero claims a coarser precision than the data supports. The error, \(\pm 0.5\) kg, is correct. This matters more here than it would elsewhere, since significant figures are the subject of this very chapter.]

[Textbook misprint: in the printed answer every zero exponent is set as a degree sign, six times over — so the dimensional formulae read \(M^{\circ}\) and \(T^{\circ}\) where \(M^{0}\) and \(T^{0}\) belong. Confirmed against the correctly-set zeros in \(v_{0}\) two lines above. The dimensions themselves are correct.]

[Textbook misprint: the question's own data are internally inconsistent. The length is given as \((4.00 \pm 0.001)\) cm, whose uncertainty is finer than the last digit of the value quoted, while the radius is \((0.0250 \pm 0.001)\) cm, whose uncertainty is ten times COARSER than its last digit. The percentage error \(8.185\%\) follows exactly from the numbers as printed and is retained; note it is quoted to four significant figures although the uncertainties carry one.]
